How to Introduce Your Indoorsy Friend to the Outdoors

By Alex Thompson | May 15, 2025 | Camp & Hike

We all have that one friend who would rather binge-watch Netflix than set foot on a trail. But getting your indoorsy friends outside doesn't have to be a battle — it just takes the right approach. Here are our favorite strategies for turning couch potatoes into happy campers.

Start Small: Easy Day Hikes

Don't throw your friend into a 20-mile backcountry trek on their first outing. Instead, pick a short, well-maintained trail with a rewarding view at the top. A 2-3 mile hike with moderate elevation gain is perfect for beginners. Look for trails near your city that offer scenic payoffs without too much suffering.

Some great beginner-friendly options:

  • Local nature preserves with paved or gravel paths
  • State parks with well-marked loop trails
  • Waterfall hikes that end at a stunning cascade
  • Coastal walks along beach cliffs

Gear Up (But Don't Overdo It)

Nothing ruins a first outdoor experience faster than uncomfortable gear. Make sure your friend has proper footwear — not flip-flops or fashion sneakers, but real hiking shoes or trail runners. REI's rental program is perfect for letting beginners try gear before investing.

Essential gear for a first hike:

  • Comfortable hiking shoes or trail runners
  • Moisture-wicking clothing layers
  • A daypack with water and snacks
  • Sunscreen and a hat
  • A trail map or downloaded offline map

Car Camping: The Gateway Drug

Car camping is the perfect introduction to sleeping outdoors. You get the campfire experience, the stargazing, and the morning coffee in nature — all with the comfort of driving right up to your campsite. Pack an air mattress, bring camp chairs, and don't forget the s'mores supplies.

Make It Social

Everything is better with friends. Plan a group outing so your indoorsy friend has company and support. Group dynamics take the pressure off any one person and create a fun, memorable experience. Plus, shared suffering (like rain on a campout) makes for the best stories later.

Focus on the Experience, Not the Miles

The goal isn't to set a speed record or bag a peak. Slow down, enjoy the scenery, and let your friend discover what makes the outdoors special at their own pace. Stop for snacks, take photos, and celebrate the small wins.

Remember: your friend might not become a wilderness enthusiast overnight, and that's perfectly fine. The key is creating a positive first experience that leaves them wanting more.
